contexts.context: The excerpt models Ti-6Al-4V powder transport through a coaxial nozzle, not auger tapping or compaction. Gas-atomized particles are spherical, 60–90 μm (D50 = 75 μm; aspect ratio >0.92), with density 4330 kg/m³. ANSYS Fluent uses steady 3D Eulerian gas flow plus a Discrete Phase Model, k–ε turbulence, gravity, and ultrasonic vibrations; interparticle collisions/coalescence are neglected. Argon flows are 4 L/min transport and 6 L/min shield. Thus, it provides evidence for spherical-particle gas-flow simulation but no validation of tapped density, single-tap mass release, irregular-shape DEM, or cohesion effects.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. How are tapping, vibration and compaction of fine powders simulated: DEM of tapped density and Hausner ratio, vibration-assisted dosing from vibrated capillaries and funnels, Monte Carlo and random-packing algorithms (Lubachevsky-Stillinger, Jodrey-Tory, random sequential addition) for packing density from a particle-size distribution, and image-based workflows that turn SEM or micro-CT particle images into DEM particles? How well do these reproduce measured bulk and tapped density and the mass released by a single tap? How are irregular particle shapes (salt crystals, water-atomized or milled powders) represented (multi-sphere, superquadric, polyhedral DEM), and how much does shape matter compared with cohesion?

contexts.context: The excerpt studies DEM powder spreading, not tapping or density validation. Real irregular PA12 particles have greater substrate/interparticle contact area than equal-volume spheres, producing higher powder-bed temperatures. At 50 versus 250 mm/s blade speed, faster spreading creates a thinner layer and higher average bed temperature after 1 s, although particles beneath the blade have less heating time. Changing temperature-dependent Young’s modulus (α=2, 20, 200) barely changes packing; α=20–200 increases softening, overlap, cohesion, and heat conduction. Shape therefore strongly affects contact-mediated behavior, while stiffness effects are also important.

contexts.context: DEM simulations found powder spreading worsens as sliding/rolling friction, cohesion (Bond number \(Bo_{50}\)), and speed increase, indicating roughness, nonsphericity, and cohesion strongly affect flow. Blade spreading reached \(MF_{\max}\approx50\%\) at 10 mm/s, falling to 20–30% at 50–100 mm/s; a counter-clockwise roller compacted powder and reached about 60%. Strong cohesion produced agglomerates, though increased sliding friction could reduce contacts and improve flow. Higher friction also caused empty patches and nonuniform layers. Roller compaction generally improved mass fraction, but behavior depended on coupled friction, cohesion, and speed.

contexts.context: The excerpt validates an image-to-particle reconstruction workflow using periodic synthetic packings: cubic and rhombohedral spheres bracket monodisperse packing densities, while random spheres and cylinders test disorder and nonsphericity. Voxel resolution strongly affects particle–contact assignment, especially at noninteger voxels-per-diameter; cylinder counts from burn extrema were 95 versus 98 actual at 10 VPD. Particle-location errors were about five times larger without optimization. Surface-area errors reached −3.3% for spheres and −12.8% for cylinders (improving to approximately −1.3% and −9%). It provides no measurements of tapped density, Hausner ratio, vibration, or mass released by a tap.

contexts.context: DEM regression for funnel discharge showed excellent fits: adjusted \(R^2=0.981\) for free-flowing powder and 0.957 for cohesive powder. Particle–particle sliding friction \(\mu_{s,pp}\) had the strongest negative effect on mass-flow rate \(\dot m\); higher friction delayed discharge. Rolling friction \(\mu_{r,pp}\) and particle diameter also reduced cohesive-powder flow, while stiffness \(Y\) slightly increased free-flowing discharge. Example simulations plotted mass and instantaneous flow rate versus time, with kinetic energy tracked every 1 ms; particles settled for 0.3 s before outlet opening.

contexts.context: The excerpt addresses statistical representation of particle arrangements, not powder tapping or dosing experiments. It defines n-point phase probabilities, \(S_n^{(i)}=\langle V_i(y_1),...,V_i(y_n)\rangle\), and particle-center densities \(f_m\), with \(f_1=n\) and volume fraction \(c=n\bar v_i\). Spatial clustering is characterized by Ripley’s \(K(r)\) function (Eq. 2), using edge corrections. Packing simulations use periodic/toroidal boundaries to reduce wall effects: particles leaving a cube re-enter through the opposite face, with 8 neighboring boxes in 2-D and 26 in 3-D. No density, tap-release, shape-model, or cohesion validation results are reported.

contexts.context: The study used Bayesian optimization to calibrate only stiffness/cohesion \(k\) and rolling friction \(\mu_r\); for larger parameter sets, orthogonal arrays or Latin hypercube sampling and “several tens” of preliminary simulations may be needed. A random-forest surrogate reduced prediction time from ~8 hours per DEM run to <1 s. Calibration yielded \(k=48{,}779.3\ \mathrm{J/m^3}\), \(\mu_r=0.60\), but parameters reproducing consolidation overestimated adhesion during spreading. Lowering \(k\) to \(15{,}833\ \mathrm{J/m^3}\) produced sparse beds consistent with experiments. Scaling matched \(\sigma/E\): 9 kPa/ \(2\times10^{11}\) Pa experimentally versus 0.225 Pa/\(5\times10^6\) Pa in DEM.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes image-informed DEM for irregular PA12 particles: SEM images are binarized, extruded into 3D, and converted using open-source CLUMP into rigid multi-spheres (example \(N_{\text{sub}}=10\)). Sub-sphere count controls morphological fidelity versus computational cost; subspheres affect contact detection, while the aggregate determines inertia and motion. Simulations use temperature-dependent Hertz–Mindlin frictional contacts. Realistic irregular and equal-size spherical particles are compared in powder spreading, assessing flowability and thermal profiles. This excerpt reports no tapped-density, Hausner-ratio, single-tap release, vibration, packing-algorithm, or quantitative shape-versus-cohesion results.

contexts.context: The paper presents a general algorithm for reconstructing particulate structure from segmented XMT/micro-CT voxel data, avoiding particle dispersion and preserving orientation, spatial correlations, porosity, and packing. A five-step workflow begins with “dual-phase burn,” identifies particle-phase extrema, refines particle locations, labels each solid voxel by particle, then computes properties. Resulting voxel-based particles provide size, volume, aspect ratio, surface area, orientation, contact areas, coordination numbers, and spatial statistics. Unlike sphere-specific center-finding methods, it handles angular and irregular materials without prior shape/size assumptions, though thresholding and segmentation remain challenging.

contexts.context: DEM models particles individually via Newton’s laws and contact forces, including friction, adhesion, and repulsion; the example used static/dynamic friction 0.3. GranOO supports spherical and nonspherical particles using GJK and bounding-box detection. Particle “rain” (about 12,000 grains, 200 nm–20 µm) followed by roller layering produced 57% packing for platelet particles, whereas measured tapped density was 42.8 ± 0.5%; the mismatch was attributed to imperfect particle morphology representation. Platelet orientation and shape strongly affected packing, and the framework could also model spheroids or needles.

contexts.context: A DEM study settled **500,000 particles** under gravity, compressed them with a servo-controlled rigid wall, and calculated void ratio. Although hexagonal-copper Young’s modulus was ~**200 GPa**, the realistic **9 kPa** consolidation pressure was reduced to **0.9 kPa** to avoid prohibitively small time steps. Bayesian optimization calibrated rolling friction (μr **0.05–0.7**) and cohesion energy density (k **10²–10⁵ J/m³**) using five initial cases plus **100 iterations**, minimizing \((e_{\rm exp}-e_{\rm DEM})^2\). The best fit was **k=47,500 J/m³, μr=0.5, void ratio=0.776**. A spreading simulation used **50,000 particles** and a blade at **25 mm/s**.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. How are tapping, vibration and compaction of fine powders simulated: DEM of tapped density and Hausner ratio, vibration-assisted dosing from vibrated capillaries and funnels, Monte Carlo and random-packing algorithms (Lubachevsky-Stillinger, Jodrey-Tory, random sequential addition) for packing density from a particle-size distribution, and image-based workflows that turn SEM or micro-CT particle images into DEM particles? How well do these reproduce measured bulk and tapped density and the mass released by a single tap? How are irregular particle shapes (salt crystals, water-atomized or milled powders) represented (multi-sphere, superquadric, polyhedral DEM), and how much does shape matter compared with cohesion?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a shaking collective rearrangement model (SCRM) for generating statistically homogeneous random particle packings. Global sequential shaking disrupts dense, “locked” local configurations and reduces RDF noise; local neighbor checks reduce computation, while optimized shake-window size minimizes trial attempts. Shaking is computationally expensive but parallelizable. The model evaluates local homogeneity using histogram fractions \(p(n_h)\), more sensitive than the K-function. Results concern identical spherical particles, with experimentally reported close-packing fractions \(c\approx0.59\)–0.64; simulations use \(n=2000\) spheres at \(c=0.575\). No tapping, DEM density, single-tap mass, irregular shapes, or cohesion comparisons are quantified.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes DEM as modeling individual grain collisions via contact detection, resolution, and time integration. Irregular grains are represented using overlapping/clustered multispheres, tetrahedra, intersecting half-spaces (polyhedra), or image-based Markov realizations from X-ray scans. Multisphere fitting can be computationally expensive and may create unrepresentative rough surfaces. PhysX enables efficient real-time simulations but trades accuracy for speed; LIGGGHTS and ChronoEngine favor accuracy. The excerpt provides no measured bulk/tapped-density or single-tap-release validation, nor a direct comparison of shape effects versus cohesion.

contexts.context: Roy et al. model powder-bed spreading with DEM using irregular particles represented by bonded multi-spheres, incorporating conduction and radiation plus temperature-dependent elastic properties. Simulations of pre-heated PA12 spread over a hot substrate show particle temperature depends on spreading speed, particle shape, and the evolving heap kinematics ahead of the blade. The introduction states irregular shape causes interlocking, frictional voids, poorer flowability, lower packing density, and rougher layers; spherical, narrow-size powders generally flow and pack better. The excerpt does not report tapped-density, vibration, single-tap mass-release, or quantitative shape-versus-cohesion validation.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents image-based DEM particle modeling using non-spherical polyhedra, balancing fidelity against computational cost through face count. Micro-CT data (2.3 µm voxels) from seven regolith simulants were segmented into triangular meshes. A stochastic model fits measured 3D particle geometries, then simulated annealing coarsens meshes while preserving selected descriptors—volume, surface area, aspect ratio, or sphericity. Sphericity is \(S=\pi^{1/3}(6V)^{2/3}/(3A)\); aspect ratio is \(AR=D_{\max}/D_{\min}\). Adhesion and roughness unresolved by imaging are incorporated through calibrated contact parameters, highlighting coupled shape/cohesion effects.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a deterministic force-biased algorithm for generating dense random packings of spheroids, including oblate and prolate shapes. It begins with randomly placed particles, then iteratively shifts, optionally rotates, and contracts them until actual packing fraction \(g_{\rm act}\) reaches a target, density convergence \(g_{\rm nom}-g_{\rm act}<\epsilon\), or an iteration limit. It distinguishes nominal density (based on total particle volume) from actual non-overlapping density, with \(g_{\rm nom}\ge g_{\rm act}\). The method produces diverse, empirically tunable packings and analyzes structure using pair-correlation functions, but does not evaluate coordination-number distribution or packing stability.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes computational generation and analysis of random, including bimodal, sphere packings. Periodic “minimum image” boundaries avoid edge effects; spherical boundaries prevent preferential directions and crystalline periodic packing. Packing structure is quantified with the radial distribution function, \(f_2(r)=n^2g(r)\), where \(g>1\) indicates clustering, \(g<1\) inhibition, and \(g\to1\) at large distances. Particle sizes/types are handled through marked or partial RDFs \(g_{km}(r)\). Its collective rearrangement model, based on Lubachevsky–Stillinger, starts random points with random velocities and grows particle radii over time, incorporating shaking to produce homogeneous, highly mixed polydisperse configurations. No tap simulations, measured densities, released mass, cohesion, or irregular-shape representations are reported.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. How are tapping, vibration and compaction of fine powders simulated: DEM of tapped density and Hausner ratio, vibration-assisted dosing from vibrated capillaries and funnels, Monte Carlo and random-packing algorithms (Lubachevsky-Stillinger, Jodrey-Tory, random sequential addition) for packing density from a particle-size distribution, and image-based workflows that turn SEM or micro-CT particle images into DEM particles? How well do these reproduce measured bulk and tapped density and the mass released by a single tap? How are irregular particle shapes (salt crystals, water-atomized or milled powders) represented (multi-sphere, superquadric, polyhedral DEM), and how much does shape matter compared with cohesion?

Multi-sphere particles are rigid assemblies of sub-spheres; increasing the number, size, and placement flexibility of sub-spheres improves shape fidelity but reduces computational efficiency. Two arrangements are considered: control geometry, in which sub-spheres remain inside the target geometry, and control volume, in which some may extend outside it to match volume. Polyhedral particles represent surfaces with vertices, edges, and planes and are considered suitable for discontinuous shapes such as coke. contexts.context: The excerpt provides background useful for comparing DEM grain-shape representations and packing algorithms, but it does not directly report a controlled experimental comparison of multi-spheres, polyhedra, and superellipsoids, nor does it discuss metal-powder spreadability or cohesion. It distinguishes geometric packing methods from dynamic DEM methods. Geometric methods are computationally fast and can assemble large packs, exemplified by Jodrey and Tory’s monodisperse spherical packing method, which converges from randomly distributed sphere centers by eliminating overlap while minimizing the pack’s outer diameter. Ballistic deposition is another geometric approach. However, such packs are commonly mechanically unstable and do not provide contact-force information. Dynamic methods assemble grains through physical forces and are more appropriate when mechanical stability and contacts matter, although they are computationally more involved. For irregular shapes, the excerpt identifies multispheres—clusters or clouds of overlapping or nonoverlapping small spheres—as a widely used approximation; internal contacts are ignored and the cluster behaves as a rigid body. It also notes research involving regularly shaped nonspherical grains, including polyhedra, while emphasizing the difficulty of modeling irregular grain position, orientation, and shape. Grain morphology affects porosity, permeability, and elastic bulk modulus. The cited software supports grain-size distributions, multiple grain types, irregular shapes, and loose or dense packs, making it potentially relevant to PSD and shape-sensitivity studies, but quantitative accuracy/cost comparisons and experimental validation details are not included here.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), not powder-flow simulation. It obtains criterion weights and alternative-performance scores through pairwise-comparison judgment matrices. Principal eigenvectors are normalized into priority vectors; consistency is checked using \(CI=(\lambda_{\max}-n)/(n-1)\) and \(CR=CI/RCI\), with \(CR<10\%\) considered adequate. Final alternative priority is \(FP_i=\sum_{j=1}^{N}PV_{ji}\times PVC_{rj}\). It acknowledges subjectivity in judgments, while consistency checks mitigate it, and notes AHP can reduce the resources required for detailed objective product modeling.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. How are tapping, vibration and compaction of fine powders simulated: DEM of tapped density and Hausner ratio, vibration-assisted dosing from vibrated capillaries and funnels, Monte Carlo and random-packing algorithms (Lubachevsky-Stillinger, Jodrey-Tory, random sequential addition) for packing density from a particle-size distribution, and image-based workflows that turn SEM or micro-CT particle images into DEM particles? How well do these reproduce measured bulk and tapped density and the mass released by a single tap? How are irregular particle shapes (salt crystals, water-atomized or milled powders) represented (multi-sphere, superquadric, polyhedral DEM), and how much does shape matter compared with cohesion?

contexts.context: The excerpt focuses on powder-bed spreading, not tapped-density or single-tap dosing simulations. It reports fines preferentially depositing at the platform start and coarse particles at the end through percolation/Brazil-nut segregation; contributors include particle size/distribution, fines concentration, shape, density, layer thickness, and spreading velocity. Even narrow-size powders segregated, changing D-values and producing an approximately “3:2” size-density ratio (Dv10–Dv50 versus Dv50–Dv90). Segregation causes local bed-density variation and melt-pool instability. Fused spatters, jamming, warping, balling, swelling, and geometry height differences further impair spreading.

contexts.context: A 2025 study calibrated DEM powder behavior using Bayesian optimization to minimize squared error between experimentally measured and simulated void ratio after 9 kPa consolidation. FT4 testing compressed nearly spherical gas-atomized Hastelloy X (mostly 10–40 µm; mean 29 µm). LIGGGHTS used Hertz–Mindlin contacts, SJKR cohesion (surface energy \(k\)), and constant-directional-torque rolling resistance (\(\mu_r\)); 500,000 particles were simulated in a 2×2×5 mm domain. Identified parameters were then transferred to powder-spreading simulations, demonstrating calibration efficiency where exhaustive DEM sweeps are computationally impractical.

contexts.context: The excerpt evaluates irregular particles using multi-sphere DEM (3–24 sub-spheres) and polyhedral DEM (4–32 planes). Experimental heap height was 6.97 cm and voidage 0.386. Multi-sphere control-geometry results were nonmonotonic: CG-6 best matched voidage (0.391; 1.3% error), while CG-24 had 8.3% error; control-volume CV-6 best matched heap height (1.1% error), though CV-24’s voidage error reached 8.8%. Polyhedral resolution improved agreement: heap-height error fell from 19.8% (4 planes) to 1.4% (32 planes). Particle mass/volume and contour strongly affected pile profiles and packing predictions.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. How are tapping, vibration and compaction of fine powders simulated: DEM of tapped density and Hausner ratio, vibration-assisted dosing from vibrated capillaries and funnels, Monte Carlo and random-packing algorithms (Lubachevsky-Stillinger, Jodrey-Tory, random sequential addition) for packing density from a particle-size distribution, and image-based workflows that turn SEM or micro-CT particle images into DEM particles? How well do these reproduce measured bulk and tapped density and the mass released by a single tap? How are irregular particle shapes (salt crystals, water-atomized or milled powders) represented (multi-sphere, superquadric, polyhedral DEM), and how much does shape matter compared with cohesion?

contexts.context: DEM simulations of powder spreading used 49 µm particles, 0.1 m/s spreading velocity, 60 µm table displacement, and nine successive layers. The simulated bed had reduced height at the start, then a maximum followed by gradual decline attributed partly to increased packing density. Particle-size distributions were nearly identical for layers 3–9, but particles “de-mix” along the spreading direction. Experiments showed identical size distributions at three locations 150 mm apart, whereas simulations covered only 4 mm; matching experiments would require ≥100 mm, beyond available computational capacity. Simulated packing density was 5.0–5.1 g/cm³, with reported standard deviations from 0.6 to 0.01 g/cm³.

contexts.context: DEM comparisons of non-spherical quartz particles found shape representation strongly affects accuracy, contact number (CN), and computational cost. Super-ellipsoids had CN <5 versus 5–6.5 for multi-spheres/polyhedra; adding sub-elements generally increased CN, while super-ellipsoid shape-index effects were minimal. Polyhedra (32 planes) best matched experiments but were computationally expensive. Multi-sphere accuracy improved with sub-spheres (control-volume better overall), though efficiency fell sharply beyond 12. Super-ellipsoids remained efficient (SE-20 was 3.5× faster than spheres) while retaining reasonable accuracy.

contexts.context: The excerpt categorizes SLS powder deposition as mechanical, electrostatic, vibratory, or miscellaneous. Mechanical systems use slot feeders, blades, rollers, bins, and pistons; rolling “performs compaction,” intended to be “comparable to tapping.” Roller adhesion and powder quantity affect layer quality. A knife system achieved 30–80 µm layers with ±5 µm accuracy. Vibratory methods improve packing efficiency before compaction and include low-frequency motor/solenoid shaker feeders, vertical down-pipes, and longitudinal, transverse, or ultrasonic excitation. The excerpt does not provide quantitative validation of tapped density, single-tap release, DEM shape models, or packing algorithms.

contexts.context: Experimental IN718 powder-bed packing density was 5.0–5.1 g/cm³, with standard deviations of 0.01–0.6 g/cm³; corresponding packing fraction was 61.2–62.4% (porosity 37.6–38.8%). DEM spreading simulations showed porosity decreasing over the first 2–3 layers, then approaching 44–45%; increasing spreader speed reduced packing density because particles had less rearrangement time and were pushed off the plate, with density/porosity stabilizing around 300–500 mm/s. Results were location-dependent, and printed-wall/recoater interactions may bias measurements. Simulating ≥100-mm multilayer regions was computationally infeasible, motivating smaller or alternative approaches such as in-situ tomography.

contexts.context: DEM simulations used Hertzian Rognon cohesive interactions, damping, sliding/rolling/twisting friction, and \(N=10^5\) particles. Friction coefficients were 0.5. Settled packing depended strongly on interactions: frictionless repulsive spheres reached \(\phi\approx0.646\) (random close packing), friction-only systems \(\phi\approx0.60\), and cohesion-only systems \(\phi\approx0.52\). Cohesion and friction separately showed little slow compaction, whereas combined frictional-cohesive grains exhibited dramatically rate-dependent settling: \(\phi_{\text{settled}}\) decreased with slower ramping toward \(\phi_{\rm ALP}=0.135\), fitted using \(A=0.300\), \(B=0.098\), and \(\tau_{\rm slow}=2.2\times10^4\).

contexts.context: The excerpt focuses on DEM and experiments of powder spreading, not tapping or density. For elongated rod particles, spreading causes alignment in the flow direction and z-axis; higher aspect ratio increases disruptive Type 2 in-plane rotations and worsens bed quality. Increasing roller speed reduces some flow-direction alignment because particles cannot respond quickly, while slightly increasing z-axis alignment. Larger spreader gaps may improve arrangement and reduce congestion. Roller spreading generally aligns particles more effectively than blades, especially at aspect ratio 2.5. Experiments qualitatively confirmed simulations, but discrepancies arose from differing conditions and tracked-particle subsets.

contexts.context: Shi et al. studied eight chemically identical limestone powders spanning particle sizes, using Jenike, ELE, Schulze ring-shear, and FT4 tests. Results were highly repeatable and broadly consistent, though FT4 produced lower yield/steady stresses because of different preshearing; Schulze–Jenike differences can reach 20%. Cohesion and friction generally decreased with size to 150 μm, while bulk density increased. Above 150 μm, cohesion slightly and friction substantially increased, attributed to particle interlocking. Removing fines reduced cohesion and density but barely changed friction. The dataset supports DEM calibration/validation of cohesive and frictional behavior.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. How are tapping, vibration and compaction of fine powders simulated: DEM of tapped density and Hausner ratio, vibration-assisted dosing from vibrated capillaries and funnels, Monte Carlo and random-packing algorithms (Lubachevsky-Stillinger, Jodrey-Tory, random sequential addition) for packing density from a particle-size distribution, and image-based workflows that turn SEM or micro-CT particle images into DEM particles? How well do these reproduce measured bulk and tapped density and the mass released by a single tap? How are irregular particle shapes (salt crystals, water-atomized or milled powders) represented (multi-sphere, superquadric, polyhedral DEM), and how much does shape matter compared with cohesion?

contexts.context: The excerpt focuses on shear-based powder characterization rather than tapping or DEM. It defines effective internal friction as the yield-locus angle used for hopper design; it generally decreases with normal stress and varies with particle size. Flowability uses \(ffc=\sigma_1/\sigma_c\): \(<1\) nonflowing, 1–2 very cohesive, 2–4 cohesive, 4–10 easy flowing, \(>10\) free flowing. Smaller particles show steeper increases in unconfined yield strength with consolidation. Shear testers were repeatable; Schulze ring-shear results were slightly higher than others. For coarse powders, roughness/shape interlocking dominates; for fine powders, cohesion governs shear strength.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes vibration-assisted powder flow and packing, including motor/solenoid feeders, vibrated vertical pipes, capillaries, funnels, and ultrasonic systems. Models account for time-dependent apparent-density increases through particle rearrangement and cluster relaxation. Hall feeders reached 2.7 G with 2.5–5 mm orifices. Capillary flow stops below a critical frequency of several hundred hertz; rate rises with frequency until an upper limit. Ultrasound near 20 kHz produced a few mg/s through 0.6–1.3 mm tubes, while specialized 125/50 µm capillaries achieved 10 µg/s for ~3 µm powders. No DEM, packing-algorithm, particle-shape, density-validation, or single-tap-release results are reported.

contexts.context: Luding, Nicolas, and Pouliquen model slow compaction using random walks through a random energy landscape: agitation/shear amplitude acts as temperature, and the landscape minimum corresponds to maximum density. Experiments with tapped monodisperse glass beads show logarithmically slow densification, typically requiring ~\(5\times10^4\) taps or shear cycles; higher shear amplitude compacts more. Changing amplitude causes rapid (<20 cycles), history-dependent density jumps. The model reproduces tapping and shear qualitatively, but explicitly does not address quantitative adjustment. It reports neither particle-shape effects nor mass released by a single tap.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides limited information relevant to the requested standards and powder-feedstock metrics. It explicitly cites ASTM B213-17, which concerns measuring metal-powder flow rate with a Hall flowmeter. The reported flowability metric is HRF, expressed in seconds per 50 g (s/50 g). For this SS316L study, solvent purification improved the B5 powder’s HRF to 29.54 s/50 g, while sieving produced stronger improvements: the 32–40 µm and 40–63 µm fractions reached 24.61 and 23.58 s/50 g, respectively. The authors state that classified powders had flowability below 30 s/50 g and compared favorably with commercial powders. The excerpt also reports circularity above 0.8 for all tests, using circularity as a measure of spheroidization. It indicates that particle-size fractionation and removal of nanoparticle “bridges” affect flowability, but it does not provide the requested ASTM B212, B527, B964, B214, B822, D7891, or D6773 details. Nor does it report spreading or tapping experiments, DEM comparisons, or a systematic analysis separating particle shape, cohesion, and size effects. Therefore, this source can support only the ASTM B213 reference and limited empirical flowability/circularity observations.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides partial information relevant to the requested standards review. ASTM B213 is associated with the Hall flowmeter, in which 50 g of powder passes through a specified funnel with a 2.5 mm orifice and the elapsed time is used to determine flow rate. The test can be conducted in static or dynamic mode, so the reported flow behavior depends on the testing configuration. ASTM B964 is cited for apparent-density measurements using a Hall apparatus and for the Carney procedure; the Carney method is used when powder cannot pass through the Hall-funnel orifice and therefore is not free-flowing. ASTM B527 is identified as an ASTM counterpart for tapped-density measurement. Tapping or vibration increases packing by temporarily reducing interparticle friction, producing a higher calculated bulk density. The excerpt specifically notes that tapped density depends on particle shape, particle porosity, and particle-size distribution. It also emphasizes that flow and spreadability are multivariate and that the relevance of any individual test to a particular process remains debated. The supplied pages do not discuss ASTM B212, B214, B822, D7891, D6773, Gibbons’s review, Shi’s limestone-shear work, experimental-versus-DEM spreading or tapping data, or quantitative shape/cohesion/size effects.

snippets: Powder flow and powder spreadability are complex multi-variate phenomena.
The former has been investigated over the last number of decades, and a number of standard methods exist to quantify and compare powders of similar materials or batches.
The Hall Flowmeter method was first developed in 1945 and is documented in the MPIF and ASTM standards (ASTM -B213, 2014; MPIF, 2019)
The procedure involves passing 50 g of powder through a funnel of specific geometry and size, the hole in the funnel is of 2.5 mm diameter.
The Carney method is a similar procedure and is used when the powder does not pass through the Hall funnel orifice
Tap density is a function of particle shape, particle porosity, and particle size distribution.
Their ASTM counterparts are (ASTM -B213, 2014; ASTM B527-20, 2020).

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies several ASTM standards relevant to metal-powder feedstock characterization. ASTM B212 measures apparent density of free-flowing powders with the Hall funnel, while ASTM B213 measures flow rate using the same apparatus. ASTM B964 covers flow rate using the Carney funnel, and ASTM B527 covers tap density. ASTM B214 specifies sieve analysis, including consecutively arranged sieves, a collection pan, agitation for fifteen minutes, and wire-mesh sizes from 5 µm to 1 mm. ASTM B822 addresses particle-size distribution by light scattering, using either liquid-dispersed powder or a carrier gas, and is suitable for particles from 0.4 µm to 2 mm. The text emphasizes that particle size affects minimum layer thickness and buildable feature size. It also warns that powder sampling and flow measurements can be affected by cohesion, moisture, segregation, vibration, and whether the powder is static or moving. Free-flowing powders may segregate by particle size during pouring or storage, complicating representative sampling. The excerpt does not discuss ASTM D7891 or D6773, detailed metric interpretation or limitations for those methods, spreading experiments versus DEM results, tapping data comparisons, or quantitative effects of particle shape, cohesion, and size.

It explicitly identifies ASTM B214 for sieve analysis, ASTM B527 for tap density, ASTM B213 for Hall-flow rate, ASTM B964 for Carney-funnel flow rate, and ASTM D7891 for shear testing with a Freeman Technology instrument. It does, however, caution that powder behavior and recycling workflows depend on specific suppliers and batches, which is relevant when comparing standardized measurements with experiments or simulations. contexts.context: The excerpt emphasizes representative powder sampling and preparation before calibration or validation. ASTM B215, ISO 3954, MPIF 01, and ISO 14488 cover dynamic/static sampling; reused powder may require 100% sampling under ASTM B215. PSD testing needs liquid dispersion/deagglomeration (ISO 14887, ASTM B821/B859). ISO/ASTM 52907, ASTM F3049, and MPIF standards guide PBF characterization. Particle properties strongly influence bulk behavior, but both must be measured because tap density, angle of repose, and PSD involve dynamic processes. Small samples can misrepresent bulk powder and fine powders are contamination-sensitive.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. How are tapping, vibration and compaction of fine powders simulated: DEM of tapped density and Hausner ratio, vibration-assisted dosing from vibrated capillaries and funnels, Monte Carlo and random-packing algorithms (Lubachevsky-Stillinger, Jodrey-Tory, random sequential addition) for packing density from a particle-size distribution, and image-based workflows that turn SEM or micro-CT particle images into DEM particles? How well do these reproduce measured bulk and tapped density and the mass released by a single tap? How are irregular particle shapes (salt crystals, water-atomized or milled powders) represented (multi-sphere, superquadric, polyhedral DEM), and how much does shape matter compared with cohesion?

contexts.context: DEM calibration should preserve the dimensionless ratio \(P_1=\sigma/E\), allowing reduced Young’s modulus and larger stable time steps; otherwise cohesion may be overestimated. At 9 kPa, simulations produced too-low void ratios because high stress caused particle rearrangement and overlap. Consolidation is dominated by normal forces and JKR cohesion, whereas spreading is governed by tangential sliding, friction, and rotation resistance. Consequently, parameters calibrated to consolidation did not reproduce spreading. The authors recommend staged, phenomenon-aware Bayesian calibration: first match consolidation under \(\sigma/E\) scaling, then recalibrate using shear-relevant observables such as bulk density, coverage, and shear metrics.

contexts.context: Eight limestone powders (median size 2.2–938 μm) tested at 5, 20, and 35 kPa showed that bulk density and cohesion increase with stress, especially for fines; internal friction was nearly stress-independent, while effective and steady-state friction angles decreased. Below ~150 μm, contact cohesion dominates: density rises and cohesion/friction angles fall with size. Above 150 μm, geometric interlocking matters; removing fines lowers density and cohesion but barely changes friction angles. RST-01 yield loci exceed FT4 results because protocols differ, emphasizing careful calibration. This excerpt reports no tapping/vibration DEM, packing algorithm, image-based workflow, shape model, or single-tap release validation.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. How are tapping, vibration and compaction of fine powders simulated: DEM of tapped density and Hausner ratio, vibration-assisted dosing from vibrated capillaries and funnels, Monte Carlo and random-packing algorithms (Lubachevsky-Stillinger, Jodrey-Tory, random sequential addition) for packing density from a particle-size distribution, and image-based workflows that turn SEM or micro-CT particle images into DEM particles? How well do these reproduce measured bulk and tapped density and the mass released by a single tap? How are irregular particle shapes (salt crystals, water-atomized or milled powders) represented (multi-sphere, superquadric, polyhedral DEM), and how much does shape matter compared with cohesion?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes DEM-based regression models predicting angle of repose (AoR) and porosity/bulk packing fraction (ε) from particle and contact parameters. Models include particle size, Young’s modulus, particle–particle static/rolling friction, cohesion, and nonlinear interaction/quadratic terms. Adjusted R² values were 0.954–0.987 for AoR and 0.915–0.991 for ε across free-flowing and cohesive powders. For free-flowing powder, calibrated DEM predicted AoR 33.4° versus experiment (deviation +1.21°) and ε 49.62% versus approximately 50% (deviation −0.76%). Results demonstrate strong nonlinear sensitivity and regression-assisted DEM calibration.

We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. How are tapping, vibration and compaction of fine powders simulated: DEM of tapped density and Hausner ratio, vibration-assisted dosing from vibrated capillaries and funnels, Monte Carlo and random-packing algorithms (Lubachevsky-Stillinger, Jodrey-Tory, random sequential addition) for packing density from a particle-size distribution, and image-based workflows that turn SEM or micro-CT particle images into DEM particles? How well do these reproduce measured bulk and tapped density and the mass released by a single tap? How are irregular particle shapes (salt crystals, water-atomized or milled powders) represented (multi-sphere, superquadric, polyhedral DEM), and how much does shape matter compared with cohesion?

# Simulating and interpreting tapping in an auger powder doser

**Bottom line.** Use the dosing fingerprint to infer *effective, device- and condition-dependent DEM parameters*, not unique intrinsic values of cohesion or friction. A useful model must reproduce several independent responses—mass per revolution, zero-flow events, release after one tap, afterflow, and packing under a specified preparation protocol. Matching mean flow alone, even without fitted parameters for salt, does not validate the contact law for cohesive powders or predict spreadability. In particular, published consolidation-calibrated cohesion parameters have produced an unrealistically cohesive simulated spread layer. (katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 9-11, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 11-14)

## 1. Tapping, vibration, and compaction

**Tapped-density DEM.** Generate particles from the measured size distribution, pour them into a model of the *actual density-test cylinder*, let them settle, and impose the measured displacement or acceleration history of each tap on the walls. After every impulse and relaxation, measure bed height and calculate bulk density. Report the full trajectory, ρ(n), as well as loose density, protocol-defined final tapped density, and **Hausner ratio = ρ_tapped/ρ_loose**. Keep fill mass, cylinder and wall material, initial pouring procedure, tap amplitude, frequency, number of taps, and relaxation criterion identical between experiment and simulation: tapping is history-dependent, not simply a request for the densest attainable packing. Classical granular-tapping experiments exhibit slow, approximately inverse-logarithmic compaction and dependence on excitation history; DEM of frictional *and* cohesive particles likewise shows unusually strong preparation-rate dependence. (ratsimba2021densificationbehaviourand pages 5-10, fernandezUnknownyeardevelopmentandevaluation pages 40-43, nan2023ultraslowsettlingkinetics pages 2-3, luding2000aminimalmodel pages 1-3)

A published GranuPack protocol illustrates what should be reproduced: a 26-mm-diameter metal cylinder was filled using a slowly withdrawn inner tube; each tap raised and dropped the cylinder **1 mm**, and bed height was recorded after each tap. For irregular, fine Y₂O₃, measured loose and tapped densities were **0.85 and 1.26 g cm⁻³**, giving **HR ≈ 1.49**. Its accompanying DEM, however, simulated *particle rain followed by roller recoating*, **not** that tap sequence; its 57% platelet-bed packing therefore cannot be claimed as a prediction of tapped density or HR. The paper also reports mutually difficult-to-reconcile relative-density figures—26.1% for its measured tapped density, 37 ± 5% for a geometrically measured recoated bed, and, later, 42.8 ± 0.5% described as tapped density. Check solid-density denominators and protocols before using any of those fractions as calibration targets. (ratsimba2021densificationbehaviourand pages 10-15, ratsimba2021densificationbehaviourand pages 5-10, ratsimba2021densificationbehaviourand pages 15-22)

**Tap-assisted dispensing is a different experiment.** In the 3-mm outlet, a solenoid impulse can both rearrange or densify the reservoir and break a local arch or adhered plug. Model the auger, outlet and PLA/PETG walls; stop the auger; equilibrate the observed fill state; apply the *measured housing acceleration waveform* at its measured location; then count particles crossing the outlet versus time. Sample independent initial configurations and report the probability of **no release**, the distribution of released mass conditional on release, latency, and post-tap afterflow. If housing flexure changes outlet clearance or wall motion, a rigid-body impulse is insufficient; measure or model that motion. For periodic vibration use a prescribed wall motion, for example z(t)=A sin(2πft), while keeping amplitude and acceleration distinct. Published vibrated-tube and capillary work reports onset thresholds and strong dependencies on frequency, amplitude and bore: a review describes several-hundred-Hz onset in one vibrating-capillary arrangement and milligram-per-second flows through approximately 0.6–1.3-mm ultrasonic capillaries. A separate experimental ultrasonic system used **28 kHz** and **0.30–0.35-mm** outlets for cohesive 10–50-µm powders. These are mechanistic analogues, **not** quantitative validation of a single solenoid tap on an auger housing. An ultrasonic gas-transport nozzle simulation located in this literature uses a dilute discrete-phase CFD model that neglects interparticle contacts; it likewise cannot validate cohesive arch breakup. (nikiforov2026numericalsimulationof pages 10-13, zhang2019laserbasedadditive pages 100-104, psarommatis2022systematicdevelopmentof pages 4-5)

The available numerical benchmarks show both promise and limitations, but are **not interchangeable validation tests**. (ratsimba2021densificationbehaviourand pages 15-22, ma2023acomparativestudy pages 13-15, ma2023acomparativestudy pages 15-18, habiba2023powderspreadingmechanism pages 15-17)

In particular, I found **no defensible measured-versus-DEM error estimate for mass freed by one tap in this specific kind of doser**. Treat that as an independent, currently unvalidated prediction rather than assigning an accuracy from tapped density, continuous vibratory feeding, or average screw flow. The quartz-sand shape benchmark in the table pertains to much larger, effectively noncohesive particles in a charging apparatus; its small voidage errors should not be transferred to fine, cohesive powders. ## 2. What a particle-size distribution can—and cannot—predict

A fast packing ensemble is valuable for initializing DEM and bounding the *geometric* contribution of size grading. Convert a volume-weighted diffraction distribution into numbers of particles in size bins, preserving their **solid volume fractions**, not assigning equal particle counts to each bin. Generate multiple finite-volume realizations and check wall effects, size segregation and the contribution of rare coarse particles near the outlet. Three distinct constructions are useful:

* **Lubachevsky–Stillinger:** move initially small hard spheres while increasing their radii in the prescribed size ratios; collisions and growth rate determine the final jammed structure. Polydisperse extensions and periodic boundaries have been described. (buryachenko2012modelingofrandom pages 4-6, buryachenko2012modelingofrandom pages 6-7)
* **Jodrey–Tory/collective rearrangement:** begin with candidate centers and iteratively resolve overlaps while compacting the configuration. This supplies dense sphere packs efficiently, but geometric packs may lack mechanically stable contacts and contact-force information. (bezrukov2006simulationandstatistical pages 2-4, ibrahim2019particulaasimulator pages 2-3)
* **Random sequential addition:** attempt nonoverlapping placements and reject unsuccessful insertions; optional later displacements or compression change the protocol and therefore the attainable packing. For irregular blocks, reported packing fractions changed appreciably with orientation and subsequent applied pressure. Thus a generated fraction is not, by itself, an ASTM tapped density. (sergi2012randompackingof pages 2-4)

Compute geometric ϕ=ΣV_particle/V_bed and, for a single fully dense constituent, ρ_bulk≈ϕρ_skeletal. For alloy mixtures, sum constituent masses and solid volumes explicitly. Then **pour and tap those generated particles with contact forces** if the desired output is loose or tapped density. A near-0.64 random-close-packed sphere baseline is not universal: an illustrative cohesive/frictional DEM study obtained approximately **0.646** for repulsive frictionless grains, **0.60** with friction alone, and **0.52** with cohesion alone under its particular preparation protocol. These are mechanism demonstrations, not predictive constants for salt, Si, or Al powders. (ibrahim2019particulaasimulator pages 2-3, nan2023ultraslowsettlingkinetics pages 2-3)

## 3. Image-informed irregular shapes

A practical image-to-DEM pipeline is **representative sampling → SEM projections or sufficiently resolved micro-CT → segmentation and separation of touching particles → particle-wise volume, equivalent diameter, aspect ratio, angularity and convexity distributions → simplified shapes → validation of shape *and* bulk responses**. SEM alone does not uniquely recover depth: one published workflow extruded binarized SEM silhouettes of PA12 powder into approximate 3D targets and used the open-source **CLUMP** generator to fit approximately **10 rigidly connected subspheres per particle**. Micro-CT provides genuine 3D geometry but introduces resolution, segmentation and contact-identification errors; a validated image-reconstruction study found that identifying nonspherical touching particles was substantially harder than identifying spheres. A newer micro-CT workflow segmented isolated regolith particles, reconstructed triangular meshes and coarsened them while preserving selected volume, area and aspect-ratio statistics. CT-resolved and sub-resolution surface roughness must be distinguished: unresolved roughness and chemistry still require effective contact parameters. (thompson2006quantitativecomputerreconstruction pages 6-8, roy2024combinedthermaland pages 3-5, thompson2006quantitativecomputerreconstruction pages 2-3, weber2026geometrypreservingmeshcoarsening pages 3-6)

For **gas-atomized Al alloys**, start with PSD-resolved spheres and measured satellites or an irregular-shape minority; for **salt crystals**, test cuboid-like superquadrics or low-face-count polyhedra; for **water-atomized, milled or visibly elongated particles**, use a small *distribution* of image-informed multispheres or polyhedra. Rigid multispheres reuse sphere-contact routines but can introduce artificial bumps and multiple contacts. Superquadrics efficiently capture rounded boxes and elongated or flattened forms but not arbitrary concavities. Polyhedra preserve facets and edges useful for crystalline/interlocking grains, at higher contact-detection cost. These are alternatives to benchmark, not interchangeable ways of assigning the same friction coefficient. In an experimental quartz-sand charging comparison, measured voidage was **0.386** versus **0.391** for a six-sphere representation, **0.398** for a 32-plane polyhedron, and **0.359** for the tested superellipsoid; increasing subsphere count did **not** monotonically improve voidage. More facets and subspheres increased computational cost, particularly above about 16 polyhedral planes or 12 subspheres in that study. (roy2024combinedthermaland pages 3-5, weber2026geometrypreservingmeshcoarsening pages 3-6, ma2023acomparativestudy pages 13-15, ma2023acomparativestudy pages 15-18, ma2023acomparativestudy pages 18-19)

**Shape versus cohesion is regime-dependent.** A comparison of chemically identical limestone powders found cohesion dominant for its finer samples, whereas for coarser samples—above roughly **150 µm** in that experiment—geometric interlocking increasingly controlled bulk friction. Removing fines reduced measured bulk cohesion while hardly changing bulk friction. DEM spreading studies likewise find that sufficiently strong cohesion can create clumps and sparse layers, while sliding/rolling resistance and shape also change coverage, alignment and heterogeneity; a roller may compact where a blade does not. Consequently, ranking shape against cohesion using one fitted angle of repose is not identifiable: evaluate a *shape × adhesion × moisture* sensitivity grid for each powder class. In particular, rolling friction used to compensate for missing angularity should be reconsidered after introducing faceted salt particles. (shaheen2020theinfluenceof pages 11-14, roy2024combinedthermaland pages 1-3, shi2018effectofparticle pages 15-17, shi2018effectofparticle pages 1-2, shi2018effectofparticle pages 17-18)

## 4. Feasible Bayesian calibration and independent checks

At **26–30 CPU-min per revolution**, a design of 100 full-revolution runs costs roughly **43–50 CPU-hours**, before replicated stochastic initial states or more expensive shapes. First fix externally measurable PSD, skeletal density, geometry, fill level and tap waveform; perform a screening design on particle–particle and particle–wall sliding friction, rolling resistance, restitution and effective adhesion. Use shorter outlet-region, gravity-pour, single-tap and shear simulations to refine parameter ranges. Fit a multi-output surrogate with predictive uncertainty and selectively add full-doser simulations where posterior uncertainty or predicted response is high. A reported Bayesian-*optimization* study required approximately eight hours per full DEM run and successfully found a **point estimate** using a surrogate, but its consolidation-only fit failed in powder spreading. Bayesian optimization of an error is **not** a posterior over material properties. (katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 9-11, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 4-6, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 2-4, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 11-14)

For actual simulation-based inference, define a powder-specific effective parameter vector θ and covariates x=(PSD/shape class, relative humidity or water content, reservoir and fill state, tilt, speed, wall material, tap impulse). Use a hierarchical likelihood combining continuous dose and density measurements with a Bernoulli or hurdle likelihood for **zero-flow increments**, a positive-mass distribution for nonzero increments and tap release, and censored/event-time treatment if afterflow ceases or is unobserved. Include balance noise, run-to-run initial-state variation, surrogate uncertainty and a model-discrepancy term; fit replicate powder preparations, and reserve complete humidity, fill, angle or powder conditions for posterior-predictive testing. Record whether mass per revolution and afterflow were measured with or without taps, rather than treating them as independent material properties. A salt prediction of 105 mg/rev is a useful held-out flow check, but does not by itself identify adhesion, wall friction or packing. Multiresponse sensitivity work shows that repose angle, porosity and mass flow respond differently to sliding friction, rolling resistance and cohesion—precisely why combining responses improves identifiability. (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 16-18, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 4-6, elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 20-21, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 11-14)

**Standards should test transferable predictions, not be assumed equivalent to DEM coefficients.** Pair the simulated preparation and stress path with ASTM **B212** apparent density, **B527** tapped density and HR; compare shear yield loci/flow functions over matched consolidation stresses with **D7891** FT4 and **D6773** Schulze ring shear; use **B213** Hall flow and **B964** Carney flow as explicitly geometry-dependent discharge checks; and use **B214** sieving plus **B822** laser diffraction for PSD. Report non-flow through a funnel as such, not as a missing flow time; obtain skeletal density independently when converting density to packing fraction. Include measured angle of repose, SEM shape/satellites, moisture by loss on drying and controlled-humidity repeat runs. Hall/Carney openings and operating conditions differ from a 3-mm printed auger outlet. FT4 and ring-shear yield loci can differ systematically because of preshear protocol; moreover, low-stress dispensing may lie below the most reliable FT4 shear regime. Do not equate a macroscopic shear-cell cohesion intercept with an SJKR surface-energy input. (fernandezUnknownyeardevelopmentandevaluation pages 40-43, shi2018effectofparticle pages 15-17, shi2018effectofparticle pages 1-2, butler2020standardsinadditive pages 8-11, groarke2021powdercharacterization—methodsstandards pages 33-38, pinotti2026additivemanufacturingof pages 204-206, groarke2021powdercharacterization—methodsstandards pages 1-5, shi2018effectofparticle pages 17-18)

Finally, validate **spreadability with an actual representative recoater and layer thickness**: measure deposited mass or relative bed density, area coverage, empty patches, surface-height variation and size segregation, and compare posterior-predictive DEM results across blade/roller speed and gap. Do not use tapped density as the spread-bed density. In one IN718 study, experimentally inferred layer packing was **61.2–62.4%**, whereas multilayer DEM tended toward **55–56%**; differing observation and simulation conditions limit that comparison. Another study found that fitting Hastelloy-X consolidation void ratio alone led to excessive modeled adhesion and an implausibly limited spread region. The doser fingerprint can therefore be a valuable *screen and prior* for alloy discovery, but its ability to forecast powder-bed quality must be established by held-out spreading experiments, particularly for irregular grains, fines and changing moisture. (shaheen2020theinfluenceof pages 11-14, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 9-11, mussatto2021influencesofpowder pages 7-10, habiba2023powderspreadingmechanism pages 15-17, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 11-14, gibbons2024metalpowderfeedstock pages 7-8)

info.query: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. How are tapping, vibration and compaction of fine powders simulated: DEM of tapped density and Hausner ratio, vibration-assisted dosing from vibrated capillaries and funnels, Monte Carlo and random-packing algorithms (Lubachevsky-Stillinger, Jodrey-Tory, random sequential addition) for packing density from a particle-size distribution, and image-based workflows that turn SEM or micro-CT particle images into DEM particles? How well do these reproduce measured bulk and tapped density and the mass released by a single tap? How are irregular particle shapes (salt crystals, water-atomized or milled powders) represented (multi-sphere, superquadric, polyhedral DEM), and how much does shape matter compared with cohesion?
